stories.topic: Why a Poker Player Loves Hoodies
stories.summary: Amit's fondness for hoodies dates to his years as a professional poker player (2010–2015). Poker is overwhelmingly math, but live games leak tells: dilating pupils, a pulsing carotid artery. So after betting he would cover his face, avoid eye contact, never smile or react, and keep the exact same posture whether bluffing or not. His own favourite read was to crack a joke and check whether the opponent's smile was genuine (comfortable) or fake (worried). He adds that a fake smile might just mean a great hand and an urgent need for the loo.
stories.insight: Since signals leak, the disciplined move is to shut the channel entirely. And reading people only lets you update your priors a little. It never gives you certainty.
stories.quote: One reliable tell I have used a lot is you try to make the person smile normally with a joke. And human beings have two kinds of smiles. There's a fake smile and a genuine smile.

stories.summary: A friend who knew Narendra Modi when he was Gujarat's chief minister told Amit this story. Modi once recounted, in tears, a childhood night when his mother was ill and hot, and he flicked the fan switch only to find there was no electricity. Her point was that Modi's understanding is purely experiential. He grasps electricity and roads because he lived them, and he made village electrification a priority. But he doesn't go beyond what he has seen. Amit doesn't blame him for not reading, given his humble background. But he says such a leader should then surround himself with experts, and he sees little evidence of that.
stories.insight: Experience only shows you the present and a narrow slice of it. Spontaneous order, positive-sum exchange and the workings of an economy can't be seen with your own eyes. They have to be read.
stories.quote: the problem is a lot of the deep truths of the world which you and I talk about all the time go beyond what you can experience with your own eyes.

stories.summary: Ajay ranks Stalin as history's second-worst monster, after Mao and ahead of Hitler. Yet he was considered extremely sophisticated and erudite. Citing Stephen Kotkin, Ajay says Stalin, language problems aside, could sit for an hour's comfortable conversation with any philosopher in the world. He had a vast library, read intensively and scribbled in his books, so his reactions survive. Amit adds Mao, a foundational thinker on guerrilla warfare. Ajay stresses that Mao actually theorized how a guerrilla force could beat the KMT rather than winging it.
stories.insight: Reading makes better citizens on average, but it is not a sufficient condition for goodness. Some of history's worst monsters were serious readers and theorists.
stories.quote: He was considered an extremely sophisticated and erudite person. He was very well read.

stories.topic: Tolstoy Sobbing Through War and Peace
stories.summary: Ajay recalls reading that while Tolstoy was writing War and Peace, he walked around his house sobbing uncontrollably because he was lost in the minds of his characters.
stories.insight: Fiction works as an empathy engine because it lets you fully inhabit another consciousness. The writer feels this at full intensity, and the careful reader gets a share of it.
stories.quote: I have read that when Tolstoy was writing War and Peace, he used to walk around his house sobbing uncontrollably because he was lost in the mind of his characters.

stories.summary: Exhausted and stressed during a six-episode shoot, Amit opened his iPad at bedtime only to keep Harold Bloom's book ready on Kindle. Searching 'Bloom' also surfaced Bloomsbury titles, including Alasdair MacIntyre's After Virtue. Suyash Rai had recommended the book long ago. Pratap Bhanu Mehta had recently praised MacIntyre over lunch, and MacIntyre had died that May. Amit read the first chapter and half the second, woke with the argument running through his head, and skipped his usual seventeen snoozes. He then read it over morning coffee instead of prepping for the episode.
stories.insight: Serendipity and pleasure, not duty, drive a real reading life. Idea books can grip you as hard as stories do, and when one does, you should embrace it.
stories.quote: I typically will hit Snooze 17 times before I get up. But I kinda jumped out of bed because I was like, I have to read the book.

stories.summary: At NIPFP, Ila Patnaik was irritated that the admin team kept bringing her decisions they could make themselves. Her rule: every time you come to ask me a question, drop a paperclip into this jar. People would walk up, deposit the clip, hang their heads in shame, and then ask. The flow of trivial interruptions fell dramatically and the team became more thoughtful. Amit's verdict: 'Ila is a paperclip minimizer.'
stories.insight: A tiny, visible ritual cost can change behaviour more than any lecture. It makes people pause and ask whether the question is really worth it. It is the same mechanism as gamifying a habit, run in reverse.
stories.quote: each time you come to me to ask me a question, you have to put one paper clip into this jar. It worked dramatically.

stories.summary: Amit's father owned the 60-volume Great Books of the Western World, most of it still wrapped. For about ten years he urged Amit to take it to Bombay, and Amit kept refusing for lack of space in his rented house. After his father died, his library of many thousands of books went to a community library, but Amit kept these sixty as a memory of his dad. The two volumes he actually reads sit on his desk: the Synopticon, Mortimer Adler's essays on themes like love, death, desire and purpose, synthesised across the whole canon.
stories.insight: Books can be kept out of love rather than use. The Synopticon also shows what thematic, cross-canon reading looks like: one quote leads you straight into another author's volume.
stories.quote: in Bombay, you know, the cost of a book is not what you pay for it, but the real estate it occupies.

stories.topic: Thirty Books for Two Gandhi Episodes
stories.summary: For his two-part Seen and the Unseen series on Gandhi with Ramachandra Guha, Amit read some thirty books: every available biography, essay and analysis. Afterwards Guha recommended Rajmohan Gandhi's The Good Boatman, a set of thematic essays on Gandhi's life, which Amit regards as a synoptical book that synthesises a lot.
stories.insight: This is synoptical reading in practice. Each new entry point into one subject makes your understanding richer than any single narrative could.
stories.quote: I read some thirty books for that. I read everything around him.

stories.summary: Amit once said, quite honestly, that he had read two hundred books in a year, and a Twitter storm followed, with people abusing him for showing off. He has never mentioned a number since, and says his count is now a fraction of that. He credits his speed to a reading habit begun at age three or four, which means forty-five years of practice.
stories.insight: Reading is not a competition. Speed is just the residue of a long habit. What matters is the time spent in a contemplative state, not the score.
stories.quote: people started shitting on me because I said quite honestly that that year I had read two hundred books.

stories.summary: Ajay confesses he reads pages slowly and has only one mode. He would like to read three times the papers and ten times the books he does. But he plays with every sentence, word and argument as he goes, and needs extreme attention and long chunks of time. He has stopped fighting it, because everything that has happened to him has come out of reading this way.
stories.insight: Depth can beat volume. There is no single right reading speed, and making peace with your own mode beats chasing someone else's numbers.
stories.quote: I'm the world's slowest reader. I read pages slowly, but I read them deeply.

stories.topic: The DC Friend and the AI Summaries
stories.summary: On a drive in DC, a friend proudly told Amit, expecting approval, that he had AI make 500-word summaries of Amit's eight-hour Seen and the Unseen episodes. He did the same for books, and felt he now knew everything in them. Amit was viscerally angry, not because it was his show but because it is such a stupid way to consume knowledge.
stories.insight: A book's value is not information transfer. It teaches you how to think, and that process has no shortcut.
stories.quote: I was literally viscerally angry, not because it's my show

recommendations.creator: Mortimer Adler and Charles Van Doren
recommendations.context: The first of three classic books Amit drew on for the 'how to read a book' section, mainly as a guide to nonfiction.
recommendations.reason: Lays out the four levels of reading (elementary, inspectional, analytical, synoptical). It also gives a concrete four-step method for analytical reading: classify the book, state its gist briefly, outline its parts, and define the problem the author is solving.

recommendations.creator: Harold Bloom
recommendations.context: Recommended explicitly 'for gentle readers' as Amit moves from nonfiction to fiction, poetry and plays.
recommendations.reason: Bloom explains what attitude each genre demands. Slow down for short stories and novels, memorize poems, and read a Shakespeare play, watch it, then read it again.

recommendations.creator: Francine Prose
recommendations.context: The third book recommended in the 'how to read' section.
recommendations.reason: Teaches you to notice the author's tools, such as why one word and not another, and how sentence length builds rhythm or immersion. Amit says this enriches reading even if you never write.

recommendations.creator: Nicholas Carr
recommendations.context: Carr's famous 2008 essay, which Amit believes was an Atlantic cover story, cited under 'reading is good for the brain'.
recommendations.reason: Argues that our shallow interaction with the internet keeps us from going deep and makes us stupider, while books pull the other way. Amit thinks things have only gotten worse since.

recommendations.creator: Nicholas Carr
recommendations.context: The 2010 book-length version of Carr's essay. Amit calls it an 'excellent book'.
recommendations.reason: A rare essay-turned-book that earns its length. It develops the case that the form of our engagement, phone or book, shapes how deeply we think.

recommendations.creator: Jim Heckman
recommendations.context: A study Amit says he and Ajay often refer to, cited when arguing that complexity of input shapes the brain.
recommendations.reason: Children aged zero to five who grow up hearing 'ten-letter words', a proxy for complex discourse, gain a layer of intelligence that can't be made up later.

recommendations.creator: Viktor Frankl
recommendations.context: Cited as 'his great book' under reading as good for the psyche.
recommendations.reason: Frankl records that for concentration-camp inmates, literature, whether held, remembered or discussed, gave solace and a sense that the present moment is not all there is.

recommendations.creator: Alasdair MacIntyre
recommendations.context: Found by accident on Kindle during the shoot. Suyash Rai had recommended it years earlier and Pratap Bhanu Mehta had recently praised MacIntyre.
recommendations.reason: Amit loved it so much he woke with its argument in his head and read it over breakfast instead of prepping. That is his living example of the joy idea books can give.

recommendations.item: Suyash Rai Embraces India's Complexity (Ep 307, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Suyash Rai
recommendations.context: Amit calls it a 'great, awesome six and a half hour episode' while explaining who first pointed him to MacIntyre.
recommendations.reason: Suyash, whom Amit regards as a great thinker, is deeply influenced by MacIntyre. The episode is a way into that mind.

recommendations.creator: James Clear
recommendations.context: Called 'his great book' in the section on building a reading habit.
recommendations.reason: Source of two ideas used in the episode. Habits are the compound interest of self-improvement. And small dopamine rewards help habits stick, like the writer who moved a hairpin between jars for every paragraph or the bodybuilder who moved marbles for every set.

recommendations.item: chickenhappyhour on Instagram (and Amit's favourite chicken video)
recommendations.context: An excited digression while warning against reaching for Instagram instead of a book. Amit promised to put the videos in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: Amit finds them 'mind blowing' and watches his favourite on loop. Ironically, it's the very distraction he says books must beat.

recommendations.item: The Paris Review Book for Planes, Trains, Elevators, and Waiting Rooms
recommendations.creator: The Paris Review
recommendations.context: Mentioned under 'choice architecture': it's fine to read several books across genres at once.
recommendations.reason: Its stories run from elevator-ride length to long-haul-flight length. That makes it ideal when you want fiction but not a novel's full immersion.

recommendations.item: The End of History and the Last Man (and the essay 'The End of History?')
recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: Cited during inspectional reading, against the trend of nonfiction books that should have stayed essays.
recommendations.reason: A rare case where the book is genuinely great and goes well beyond the essay it grew from.

recommendations.item: Understanding Gandhi, Parts 1 and 2 (Eps 104–105, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ramachandra Guha
recommendations.context: Amit's example of synoptical reading.
recommendations.reason: For these episodes he read some thirty books on Gandhi, so they distil a whole shelf of biographies and analyses.

recommendations.creator: Rajmohan Gandhi
recommendations.context: Recommended to Amit by Ramachandra Guha after the Gandhi episodes. Amit calls it a 'great book'.
recommendations.reason: Its thematic essays on Gandhi's life synthesise a vast amount of material. Amit holds it up as a model synoptical book.

recommendations.item: Great Books of the Western World (especially the Synopticon volumes)
recommendations.creator: Mortimer Adler (editor)
recommendations.context: His late father's 60-volume set. The two Synopticon volumes sit on Amit's desk.
recommendations.reason: Adler's thematic essays on death, love, desire, purpose and agency draw on the entire canon. Amit says they fill him with 'awe' and 'joy', and send him to read the original authors.

recommendations.item: How Should One Read a Book?
recommendations.creator: Virginia Woolf
recommendations.context: First on Amit's list of further reading on the subject, offered instead of end-of-show recommendations.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great essay on exactly this episode's question.

recommendations.creator: E. M. Forster
recommendations.context: Part of Amit's further-reading list. Written in 1927.
recommendations.reason: It gives a great insight into a great novelist's mind.

recommendations.creator: Italo Calvino
recommendations.context: Part of Amit's further-reading list.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it an excellent book on the case for the classics.

recommendations.creator: James Wood
recommendations.context: A book Amit says he 'absolutely loves', from his further-reading list.
recommendations.reason: Useful for readers, not just writers. It explains voice and how the modern novel evolved, including Flaubert's role. Amit promises it 'will transform the way you read a book'.

recommendations.item: The Pleasures of Reading in an Age of Distraction
recommendations.creator: Alan Jacobs
recommendations.context: The recent book that closes Amit's further-reading list.
recommendations.reason: A contemporary take on reading well amid the distractions this episode keeps fighting.

recommendations.item: Lessons from an Ankhon Dekhi Prime Minister
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column, retold as his first reason to read.
recommendations.reason: Develops the argument that purely experiential understanding can't reach the deep, complex truths about the world. Only reading can.

recommendations.item: Ezra Klein interviewed by David Perell
recommendations.creator: Ezra Klein and David Perell
recommendations.context: Ajay recalls a recent conversation with Ezra Klein on the gap between a sophisticated thousand-word AI summary of a book and actually reading it. The show notes link this interview.
recommendations.reason: Ajay says it 'goes to the core' of why we read. The payoff is the hours of grappling with an author, not a summary.

recommendations.item: Susan Thomas's book club in Bombay
recommendations.creator: Susan Thomas
recommendations.context: Plugged right after the advice to find a community of readers.
recommendations.reason: An in-person reading community in Bombay. Joining one is the ultimate way to design your environment for reading.

recommendations.context: Demoed in the final chapter. Amit calls it 'an awesome app' based on the Zettelkasten note-taking system.
recommendations.reason: He loves two features. Nested entries let you drill from chapter to point to quote. Bidirectional linking turns any bracketed term into a clickable hub that gathers every related note. Together they replaced his scroll-and-Ctrl-F Word documents.

recommendations.item: Being Muslim in India (Ep 216, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ghazala Wahab
recommendations.context: Used in the Roam demo, which shows his notes on Ghazala Wahab's book Born a Muslim.
recommendations.reason: Shows chapter-by-chapter note-taking in action. The book also supplies a 'beautiful example of Show Don't Tell' that Amit reads out.

recommendations.item: Womaning in India With Mahima Vashisht (Ep 293, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Mahima Vashisht
recommendations.context: The second Roam demo: over a hundred newsletter posts with no ready-made structure.
recommendations.reason: Shows how building your own themes layer turns a pile of material into a map of the territory, and how that made a thematic conversation possible.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The hosts' course. Its community runs multiple book clubs, and its 'one life versus many lives' theme came up early in the episode.
recommendations.reason: A ready-made reading community, which the episode argues makes the habit far easier to keep.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's writing course. Its 'just be it' framing and a webinar on words, sentences and paragraphs both surface in the episode.
recommendations.reason: Its community ran remote fiction and nonfiction book clubs on the last Saturday of each month. It also teaches the read-like-a-writer attention to sentence choices.

core_ideas.concept: Connect More Dots: Books Give You Many Lives
core_ideas.explanation: We paint pictures of the world by connecting dots, and more dots mean a higher-definition picture. Experience gives you only the present and a narrow slice of it. Spontaneous order, positive-sum exchange and the complexity of an economy can't be seen. Ajay's framing: a practical doer reaches seventy with one life's knowledge, while a reader taps hundreds or thousands of lives.
core_ideas.quote: we paint pictures of the world by connecting dots. The more dots we have, the more high definition our picture.

core_ideas.concept: The Quality of Leisure Shapes the Brain
core_ideas.explanation: Scrolling and reading can both look like time-pass, but scrolling hops from factoid to factoid without building anything. Reading forges connections. Citing Nicholas Carr, neuroscientist Maryanne Wolf, and London cabbies whose brains rewired once they stopped memorising routes, Amit argues that the structure of what you engage with changes your brain. A richer vocabulary also means more dots: Wittgenstein held that our understanding is limited by language.
core_ideas.quote: in the first one, I'm in a shallow state of mind.

core_ideas.explanation: Reading, especially fiction, lets you feel pain that would never happen to you, which expands what Martha Nussbaum calls narrative imagination. Faced with a curt colleague, you can assume he's an asshole, or imagine he's preoccupied with work. The second reading replaces reptile-brain ego with understanding and deepens relationships. Ajay argues fiction is the prime engine of this; Amit agrees but says good biography does it too. So read both, and don't take a utilitarian, facts-only view of reading.
core_ideas.quote: George Eliot called reading the nearest thing to life.

core_ideas.explanation: In dark times literature works like therapy, as Frankl saw in the camps. It also holds up a mirror. Seeing a character feel what you thought was unique to you exposes your private and even secret self, in the sense of Gabriel García Márquez's public, private and secret selves. That is how reading answers the Greek command to 'know thyself'.
core_ideas.quote: literature kind of tells us two things. It tells us that we are not alone. And it tells us that this too shall pass.

core_ideas.explanation: In a funk we see the world through one prism, and reading, which Schopenhauer called thinking with someone else's head, offers others. Learning to be alone without being lonely is an essential skill, and books provide that companionship. Harold Bloom: imaginative literature is otherness, and so it alleviates loneliness.
core_ideas.quote: Reading is actually what can save solitude from loneliness.

core_ideas.concept: Reading as a Civic Good: Necessary, Not Sufficient
core_ideas.explanation: Following Tocqueville, democracy needs informed citizens, not just voters, and reading is how people get informed. Ajay adds that a reader imposes a positive externality, making the people around them think and debate better. But the hosts flag the limit: Stalin and Mao were serious readers and theorists. Reading is not a guarantee of goodness.
core_ideas.quote: By reading we impose a positive externality upon the world.

core_ideas.explanation: Aspiring writers who don't read have a training corpus that is too small. Creativity works on what you've absorbed. Someone who has heard a million songs writes better songs than someone who has heard a hundred, not by copying but because their subconscious has learned the forms. Even mindless reading teaches by osmosis. Ajay returns to the metaphor at the end: the payoff of reading is that you're training your LLM.
core_ideas.quote: Because your LLM, as it were, is too small.

core_ideas.explanation: Every species communicates, but only humans carry that conversation across time. Through books you can argue with Plato, Adi Shankaracharya or a dead author a continent away, the way Ajay felt James C. Scott berating him in Seeing Like a State. Without books there are no giants' shoulders to stand on.
core_ideas.quote: humans are the only species who can carry this across time.

core_ideas.concept: A Latticework of Models: Everything Is Everything
core_ideas.explanation: One or two mental models can't explain a reality this complicated. Reading builds Charlie Munger's 'latticework of models': incentives here, anthropology there, natural selection, genetics, the cinema of an era. The disciplines are silos only in name, since all of them study the human condition. That insight is where the show's name comes from.
core_ideas.quote: the show is called Everything Is Everything because of that. That the more you read, the more you realize the interconnectedness of everything

core_ideas.concept: Habit Over Targets, Identity Over Goals
core_ideas.explanation: Don't set targets like 'I'll finish that prize-winner'. Build a habit, which James Clear calls the compound interest of self-improvement. Be bloody-minded for about three months, until the loop is hardwired in the basal ganglia and feels automatic. Better still, start from identity. Ask who the best version of you is. If that person reaches for a book instead of a phone, actions flow from that self-image and a missed day doesn't break you.
core_ideas.quote: there's a great Nike slogan, just do it... But my slogan for you would be just be it.

core_ideas.concept: Engineer the Habit: Small, Frequent, Anchored, Designed
core_ideas.explanation: Start small: two pages or fifteen minutes. Favour frequency over duration. Anchor reading to an existing routine such as morning coffee, the commute or bedtime, because neurons that fire together wire together. Design your environment: keep books everywhere, put Kindle up front and delete social apps, or use a dedicated device. Ajay's version is an old iPad with only a book reader and a throwaway account. Pre-decide what you'll read next to avoid decision fatigue, the way Ajay runs 'the planner code' once each morning and then just executes. Gamify with small rewards. And find a community of readers.
core_ideas.quote: Frequency matters more than duration.

core_ideas.explanation: Elementary reading means understanding the sentences. Inspectional reading is a first date with the book: table of contents, preface, a skim to see whether it's really an essay padded into a book, as many modern nonfiction books are. Analytical reading means chewing: classify the book, state its gist in a line, outline its parts, and name the problem the author is solving. Synoptical reading means reading many books on one subject, say Bernanke, Minsky, Friedman, Keynes and the Austrians on financial crises, until the picture deepens.
core_ideas.quote: Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested.

core_ideas.explanation: When a subject grabs you, don't stop at one book. Chase the footnotes, look up the people mentioned, ask ChatGPT, check Wikipedia, and buy the next book. These detours are not digressions. They are how knowledge gets rich.
core_ideas.quote: entering rabbit holes is great. Do not think of these as digressions and a waste of time.

core_ideas.concept: Read Fiction, Poems and Plays Differently
core_ideas.explanation: Following Bloom, never skim fiction. Short stories favour the tacit and make you discern what the writer leaves out (show, don't tell; Hemingway's iceberg). A novel becomes a different book for each reader, and it pays to ask whether the characters change and why. Memorize poems, because poetry lives in rhythm. Read a Shakespeare play, watch it, then read it again. Reading like a writer adds attention to form: clipped hard-boiled sentences for action, Saramago's pages-long sentences for immersion.
core_ideas.quote: there is a beauty in that that first you belong to the poem and then the poem belongs to you.

core_ideas.concept: Format Doesn't Matter; the Words Do
core_ideas.explanation: Paper, Kindle, phone or audiobook is just packaging. Insisting on physical books shows nostalgia, not love of literature. Audiobooks are a somewhat different experience because you can't easily pause and reread, but they let people with no quiet time, like a commuter hanging on a local train, still spend that time with words.
core_ideas.quote: Literature is words. That's what they are. Everything else is packaging.

core_ideas.concept: Quit Books Freely: Your Lifetime Book Budget
core_ideas.explanation: Multiply an optimistic life expectancy by an optimistic books-per-year figure. That is roughly the most books you'll ever read, a pitiful fraction of what exists. So drop books you aren't enjoying without sunk-cost guilt, even celebrated prize-winners. And don't be a snob: an airport bestseller or an academic paper is fine if it brings enjoyment or enlightenment.
core_ideas.quote: don't throw good money after bad, as it were, don't throw good time after bad.

core_ideas.explanation: Book counts are meaningless. What matters is time spent in the contemplative, processing state that reading induces. Five books a year is fine, and speed is just the residue of a long habit. Don't even keep score.
core_ideas.quote: There is no Olympics of reading.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay compares it to eating healthy, which is nearly impossible for one person in a household full of junk food. Modern nutrition thinking changes the whole food environment instead. Likewise, reading thrives in a community of family and friends, a book club, or group viewings of the show that pause at each chapter break to argue. Arguing turns passive consumption into active learning and makes the knowledge your own.
core_ideas.quote: think of the battle of reading well, and it is harder to do it alone.

core_ideas.explanation: A thousand-word AI summary lets you sound sophisticated at a cocktail party, and you'll forget most details of a book within a month anyway. The point is the ten to twenty hours of intimate conversation with one great mind: grappling, disagreeing, having aha moments. That changes your brain and even your character. Information is trivial and you can look it up.
core_ideas.quote: I viscerally reject the word information in connection to books. Books are not information.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's Roam workflow starts by making the book's chapters top-level entries, then nesting every point and quote beneath them. Bracketed tags create bidirectional links that gather related quotes across sources. When material has no structure, like Mahima Vashisht's hundred-plus newsletter posts, he builds his own themes layer: controlling female sexuality, stereotypes, a world designed by men. The result isn't just notes but a framework for the whole subject.
core_ideas.quote: Now earlier I would have sixty pages of Microsoft Word.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit opens an episode on reading by parsing his own sentence: 'What does it mean to say I'm a huge fan of hoodies? It means two things. One, I'm huge, and two, I'm a fan of hoodies... So you see, a careful reading will reward you with additional meaning and layers.'
Amit, announcing his eleven reasons: 'I'm not scared of taking a number because Ajay can't count, but Amit can.'

After Ajay explains that Mao theorized his way into guerrilla warfare, Amit says: 'Kinda like you, Ajay Shah, right? You theorize about the world and then you do a YouTube show.' Ajay: 'Those who can do, the others become podcasters.'
Amit on communication between species: 'Dogs will bark to each other, cats will meow to each other, especially while confessing, you'll have meowpas.'
After Ajay's story of Tolstoy sobbing through War and Peace, Amit suggests another reason to sob: no air conditioning. Then he remembers it was Russia and wonders aloud whether they even had heating.
Amit, voicing a viewer: 'Ajay Shah recommended Seeing Like a State on that very cool YouTube show, and so far I've been watching it for his sex appeal and his shirts and Amit's deep, dulcet tones.'
On abandoned reading goals: 'fifth day you're like, I'm not a books kind of person, I'm a Netflix kind of person, or a Netflix and chill kind of person if you're adequately gregarious.'
Amit says 'Frequency matters more than duration', and Ajay laughs. Amit: 'You thought of sex again.' Ajay: 'Bro. Frequency matters more than duration. What else can I think of?'
On removing competition to reading: 'If you're living with other people, start living alone. I'm kidding. You know, why are you nodding?'

On James Clear's bodybuilder who moved a marble between jars for every set: 'one sincerely hopes he never dropped his weights on his head because then he might have lost his marbles... I keep making this joke. People keep laughing, I don't know why.'
Amit on Ila Patnaik's jar: 'in AI they run this famous thought experiment about the paperclip maximizer. It turns out that Ila is a paperclip minimizer.'
Introducing Reading Like a Writer: 'the third book I want to recommend for you is by Francine Prose, aptly named.'
Amit demonstrates immersive long sentences with one of his own, ending '...and you are them and they are you, and see what a long sentence this was.'
On viewers pausing the show to argue, Amit worries they might be saying 'Ajay is so sexy, why is Amit on the show. How would the show look with two Ajays talking to each other?'
In the Roam demo, Amit lets a secret out: listeners of The Seen and the Unseen are impressed that Amit has all the quotes at his fingertips. 'No, bro. I'm kind of reading them out from this.'

Ajay quotes a hard-boiled fiction line, 'She had a smile that never reached her eyes'. Amit can't place which of 'those hard-boiled fiction boys' wrote it, and later names Dashiell Hammett and Raymond Chandler as masters of terse action prose. Ajay adds the craft trick: a run of short sentences makes one elaborate sentence come alive.
Montaigne: 'I have no more made my book than my book has made me', used for reading as self-discovery.
Tocqueville's point that democracy works only if citizens are well informed, extended by Amit from free speech to reading habits.
Harold Bloom: 'Information is readily available. Where is wisdom to be found?' Also: 'Imaginative literature is otherness and as such alleviates loneliness.'
Schopenhauer on reading as thinking with someone else's head instead of one's own.
Kurt Vonnegut, as Amit recalls him: in every story, somebody has to want something. All literature is a transition between states, with conflict at its heart.

Hemingway's iceberg theory and 'show, don't tell', illustrated by Amit's image of himself at a window as the light fades and his tea goes cold, undrunk. Ghazala Wahab's grandfather offers another: he shelled pine nuts all day to reward the grandkids with fistfuls in the evening, rather than her writing 'he loved us'.
Robert Towne's Chinatown, offered as a screenplay worth reading the way Bloom says to read Shakespeare.
'Neurons that fire together, wire together', which is why a song can bring back the memory of a first kiss, or a first slap, and why anchoring reading to existing routines works.
Zettelkasten, the German note-taking system that Roam Research is based on.
